title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is in the data-collection stage of model development, not in the deployed product's real-time behavior. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files available on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified specific sources including YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. The systems were then capable of reproducing recognizable portions of specific copyrighted recordings when prompted, which record labels demonstrated by generating outputs that replicated passages from named artists. No licensing or rights-clearance process was in place before the training data was assembled.

This is a case of a system trained on material gathered without the consent of rights holders, deployed commercially, and later found to reproduce that material in its outputs. The failure would have required intervention at the data-curation stage, before training began, either through licensing agreements or filtering of protected works. The absence of any disclosed training corpus made it impossible for outside parties to assess the scope of the problem until litigation forced partial disclosure.

What is not established: the lawsuits, class actions, and the German court ruling in favor of GEMA are legal proceedings at various stages, and allegations of intentional infringement or specific financial harm remain claims rather than settled findings, except where a court has ruled or a settlement has been reached, as reported in the cases involving Warner Music Group and Universal Music.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The companies are accused of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their models and then directly reproducing sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a massive list of scraped works, featuring artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, and many others. The labels demonstrated the problem by using specific prompts to regenerate versions of copyrighted songs, successfully replicating pieces from artists like Chuck Berry and Green Day.

The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and in Massachusetts against Suno. Both companies previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use, but have refused to disclose which specific songs they trained their models on. The record labels also submitted a thumb drive containing AI-generated music examples as evidence. The lawsuits represent a major legal battle over how generative AI services can use existing creative works to train their systems, with implications extending beyond music to art, video, and text generation.
